<document>
# Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

*Review of Work and Employment Research. S. Achterberg, N. Iwu, F. Castell and J. Moreno. Review protocol registered before search.*

## Abstract

We systematically reviewed studies of reductions in scheduled working time of at least 10% with pay maintained, reporting a quantitative measure of output. Twenty-three studies (1998–2025; about 41,000 workers) met inclusion criteria. Pooled across studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0), with very high heterogeneity (I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4). Study design, the hours measure and the type of work explain much of the heterogeneity: controlled studies found smaller effects (+8.2%) than uncontrolled before–after studies (+18.7%), studies using actual hours found smaller effects (+7.9%) than those using scheduled hours (+16.6%), and per-worker output fell substantially in coverage-bound work (−8.9%) but not in discretionary work (+0.6%). There is evidence of small-study bias; adjusting for it reduces the pooled per-hour estimate to +9.1%. Effects show no sign of decay over time.

## Methods

**Search and inclusion.** We searched four bibliographic databases and two working-paper repositories, and contacted authors of known pilots. Studies were included if they (a) evaluated a reduction in scheduled hours of at least 10% with no reduction in pay; (b) reported output per worker or output per hour, or data from which either could be derived; and (c) had at least 50 workers. We excluded studies reporting only self-rated productivity. Of 412 records screened, 23 studies met the criteria.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome is the change in output per hour, expressed as a log ratio and converted back to a percentage for reporting. Where a study reported both scheduled and actual hours, we used actual hours. The secondary outcome is the change in output per worker. For controlled studies we used the difference relative to the comparison group; for uncontrolled studies, the change from baseline.

**Coding of work type.** Two coders independently classified each study's setting as *discretionary* (output can be produced at any time within a deadline: case processing, professional services, software, back-office work), *coverage-bound* (output depends on staff being present while demand arrives: counters, contact centres, retail floors, care rotas), or *mixed/unclear*. Agreement was high (κ = 0.84); disagreements were resolved by discussion.

**Synthesis.** Random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation; moderators examined by meta-regression. Small-study effects assessed by funnel plot, Egger's regression test, and trim-and-fill.

## Included studies

Of the 23 studies, 9 had a comparison group (3 randomised, including the Varden County trial; 6 matched or difference-in-differences) and 14 were uncontrolled before–after designs, including the Halden multi-organisation pilot. Eight studies measured actual hours; 15 used scheduled hours only. Thirteen settings were coded discretionary, 7 coverage-bound and 3 mixed or unclear. Only two studies were in manufacturing, both in the mixed category. Follow-up ranged from 3 to 30 months (median 6). Output measures were record-based in 12 studies and manager-reported in 11.

## Results

### Pooled effects

Across all 23 studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0; I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4; I² = 74%). The prediction interval for output per hour runs from −4% to +34%, meaning that a new study in an unknown setting could plausibly find anything from a small loss to a very large gain.

### Moderators

**Table 1. Subgroup estimates of the change in output per hour and output per worker**

| Subgroup | k | Output per hour | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| **All studies** | 23 | +13.4% (8.1 to 19.0) | −1.8% (−4.9 to +1.4) |
| Controlled designs | 9 | +8.2% (4.0 to 12.6) | −4.1% (−7.6 to −0.5) |
| Uncontrolled before–after | 14 | +18.7% (11.2 to 26.7) | −0.2% (−4.0 to +3.8) |
| Actual hours measured | 8 | +7.9% (3.6 to 12.4) | −3.9% (−7.8 to +0.1) |
| Scheduled hours only | 15 | +16.6% (9.9 to 23.7) | −0.6% (−4.3 to +3.3) |
| Record-based output | 12 | +9.7% (5.0 to 14.6) | −3.6% (−7.2 to +0.2) |
| Manager-reported output | 11 | +17.8% (10.0 to 26.1) | +0.4% (−3.9 to +4.9) |
| Discretionary work | 13 | +15.1% (8.8 to 21.8) | +0.6% (−2.8 to +4.1) |
| Coverage-bound work | 7 | +6.2% (1.1 to 11.6) | −8.9% (−13.1 to −4.5) |
| Mixed or unclear | 3 | +12.0% (−1.5 to 27.4) | −2.9% (−10.6 to +5.4) |

In a multiple meta-regression including design, hours measure and work type together, all three moderators remained associated with the effect, and together they explained 58% of between-study variance. The design and measurement moderators overlap heavily: 12 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours, and 9 of the 14 used manager-reported output. Our data cannot fully separate them.

The work-type moderator is the clearest for the per-worker outcome. In discretionary work, output per worker was essentially unchanged in pooled estimates; in coverage-bound work, it fell by about 9%, consistent across all seven studies (I² = 22%). The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work was real but too small to compensate for the hours lost.

Note that the discretionary estimate of +15.1% per hour mixes controlled and uncontrolled studies. Restricting to the five controlled discretionary studies, the per-hour estimate is +9.6% (4.8 to 14.6) and the per-worker estimate −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2).

### Small-study effects

The funnel plot is asymmetric, with small studies reporting larger per-hour gains (Egger's test p = 0.02). Trim-and-fill imputes five missing studies on the left of the funnel and reduces the pooled per-hour estimate from +13.4% to +9.1% (95% CI 3.9 to 14.6). We interpret this as evidence that small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published or publicised than small, unfavourable ones.

### Duration

Four studies reported follow-up beyond 12 months. Their pooled per-hour gain was +14.0% (95% CI 6.2 to 22.4), indistinguishable from the overall estimate. Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside.

### Mechanisms

Eleven studies measured fatigue or wellbeing alongside output. Across these, the study-level correlation between the improvement in fatigue scores and the per-hour gain was weak (r = 0.18). Only three studies measured time spent in meetings, and none tested meetings as a mediator under a registered plan; we cannot assess this mechanism. Sick leave fell in all 14 studies that reported it (pooled −31%), and staff turnover fell in all 9 that reported it.

## Discussion

The literature supports a gain in output per hour from reduced working time, but a considerably smaller one than headline pilots suggest. The figure most often quoted, a gain of more than 20%, comes from uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours and manager-reported output; each of those features is associated with larger estimates. Controlled studies, studies measuring actual hours, studies using records, and the bias-adjusted estimate converge on a gain of roughly 8 to 10%.

Whether that gain is "enough" depends on the type of work. In discretionary settings the evidence is compatible with output per worker being maintained or falling slightly; in coverage-bound settings it falls clearly, and maintaining service would require additional staff.

We do not find support for the claim, made in one re-analysis of the Halden pilot, that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact. The controlled and actual-hours subgroups, which avoid the problems that re-analysis identified, still show gains whose confidence intervals exclude zero. Nor do we find support for the claim that reduced hours are sector-general.

## Limitations

Twenty-three studies is a small base for a meta-regression with three correlated moderators. Most studies are short. Only nine are controlled, and the controlled studies are themselves mostly in the public sector. Manufacturing and shift-based production are almost absent. Classification of work type, though reliable between coders, imposes a binary on what is often a mix within a single organisation.

response:
# Critical Reading: Achterberg et al., Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

This is the most useful document of the four. It looks at the field as a whole and asks which study features predict larger effects, which is the right question. Its main conclusions are well judged: the per-hour gain is real but modest (roughly 8–10%), the large headline figures come from weaker designs, the "artifact" and "sector-general" claims are both rejected, and outcomes depend on the type of work. Its weakest claim is the one about duration. There are also some reporting and method gaps.

## What it does well

- **It identifies the moderators that the earlier documents argued about.** Design, the hours measure, the output measure and work type each predict effect size, in the expected direction.
- **It defines work type by mechanism, not sector.** The discretionary versus coverage-bound split follows Varden's logic and is coded reliably (κ = 0.84).
- **It reports a prediction interval** (−4% to +34%). This is more honest than the pooled point estimate about what a new adopter could expect.
- **It notes when subgroups overlap.** It says the design and measurement moderators can't be separated, and it gives the controlled-only estimate for discretionary work.
- **It assesses both earlier claims fairly.** It rejects "entirely artifact" and "sector-general" with reasons.

## Consistency check

Output per worker divided by output per hour should roughly equal the hours ratio. The subgroups are pooled separately, so the identity won't hold exactly, but they should be plausible:

| Subgroup | Implied hours change |
|---|---|
| All | 0.982 / 1.134 → −13.4% |
| Controlled | 0.959 / 1.082 → −11.4% |
| Uncontrolled | 0.998 / 1.187 → −15.9% |
| Actual hours | 0.961 / 1.079 → −10.9% |
| Scheduled hours | 0.994 / 1.166 → −14.8% |
| Coverage-bound | 0.911 / 1.062 → −14.2% |
| Controlled discretionary | 0.973 / 1.096 → −11.2% |

These are internally coherent. Studies that measured actual hours show smaller hours reductions than studies that used scheduled hours, as Varden and Varga & Holm would predict. Scheduled-only studies imply an average scheduled cut of about 15%, which fits a mix of 10–20% reductions. I found no arithmetic errors.

## Issues

### 1. The duration finding is the weakest claim, and the abstract overstates it

"Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside" rests on four studies, compared with the other studies rather than tracked over time within each study. That comparison has several problems:

- **Survivorship.** Pilots that go well are the ones that get extended and followed up. Failing pilots stop. Long follow-up is likely to select for success, which is the same attrition problem Varga & Holm found in Halden, now at the level of whole studies.
- **Confounding with design.** If the four long studies are uncontrolled or used scheduled hours, their inflated estimates could hide decay. The paper doesn't say what designs they used.
- **Imprecision.** The CI of 6.2 to 22.4% is consistent with substantial decay from a higher starting point.
- **The wrong test.** Decay should be tested by following the same studies over time and checking whether the gain shrinks. A between-study comparison can't do that.

"No evidence of decay in four longer studies, which cannot exclude it" would be supportable. "Set aside" is not. This matters because the duration finding is the only reply the review makes to Varga & Holm's novelty argument (see point 6).

### 2. The headline pooled estimate is the one the review argues is inflated

The abstract leads with +13.4%. That figure pools all 23 studies, including those the review shows are biased upward. The discussion then says the better estimate is 8–10%. The abstract should lead with the controlled, actual-hours or bias-adjusted estimate. Otherwise the 13.4% will be quoted as the meta-analytic answer.

Relatedly, the controlled studies show a **statistically significant fall in output per worker** (−4.1%, CI −7.6 to −0.5). The abstract instead reports the non-significant all-studies figure (−1.8%).

### 3. The "convergence" on 8–10% is less independent than it sounds

The discussion says controlled studies, actual-hours studies, record-based studies and the bias-adjusted estimate "converge" on 8–10%. But these subgroups largely contain the same studies. The actual-hours studies are probably mostly the controlled ones, and the same applies to record-based output. This is mostly one group of studies counted several ways, not several independent confirmations.

The subgroup that would be most informative is not reported: **controlled, actual hours and record-based output together.** It would be small, but it is the best evidence available.

### 4. The small-study adjustment is unreliable here

When heterogeneity is this high (I² = 81%), funnel asymmetry, Egger's test and trim-and-fill are all known to be unreliable. More specifically, the small studies are probably the uncontrolled pilots that used scheduled hours and manager reports. The asymmetry could then reflect **real design differences rather than publication bias**. The review offers publication bias as its interpretation without considering this. The +9.1% adjusted figure depends on imputed studies and should not be used as an independent estimate.

### 5. How Varden was coded is unclear

Varden contains one discretionary stratum and one coverage-bound stratum, and that contrast is its most useful feature. The counts (13 + 7 + 3 = 23) suggest each study was coded once. Then either:

- Varden was coded "mixed", which wastes its key contrast, or
- its strata were split, in which case k should be 24, and two non-independent estimates from one trial have been entered as separate studies.

The paper should say which. The same question applies to Halden, which covered six sectors, including retail.

### 6. The rebuttal of Varga & Holm is only partly successful

The review is right that controlled and actual-hours studies avoid the **measurement and organisation-selection** problems. On those points, the rebuttal works.

It does not answer the other two:

- **Novelty.** Controlled studies are not protected from it, since staff in the treated group still know they are being treated. The only reply is the duration finding, which is weak (point 1).
- **Attrition.** Withdrawals and dropouts are not coded at all. No formal risk-of-bias tool is reported either (for example ROBINS-I for non-randomised studies). For a review whose conclusions rest on study quality, that is a notable gap.

A fairer conclusion: the "entirely artifact" claim is rejected on measurement and selection, but novelty remains an open alternative.

### 7. The per-hour "gain" in coverage-bound work probably isn't productivity

The review says the +6.2% per-hour gain in coverage-bound work "was real but too small to compensate". As with Varden's counter stratum, the most likely explanation is **higher utilisation**: fewer staff serve the same flow of demand, so each is busier. That would show up as more output per hour without any improvement in effort or efficiency.

Per-worker output in this kind of work is also limited by demand, so the right outcome would be service levels (waiting times, abandonment). Those aren't synthesised.

### 8. The mechanism evidence is too thin to support even the weak conclusion

The fatigue–productivity correlation is r = 0.18 across 11 studies. Its 95% CI runs from roughly −0.45 to +0.68. The fatigue measures differ between studies, and a study-level correlation says little about individual workers. The review says "weak", which is fair, but readers could take that to mean fatigue doesn't matter. The data simply can't tell.

On sick leave, "fell in all 14 studies" is vote counting, and most of those studies were uncontrolled. The pooled −31% fits Halden (−36%, uncontrolled) and Varden (−29%, controlled), so it is probably real. The review should still separate controlled from uncontrolled studies here, as it does for output.

### 9. Other limitations, mostly acknowledged

- Three moderators in a meta-regression of 23 studies risks overfitting. The 58% variance explained should be treated with caution.
- The controlled studies are mostly public sector, and manufacturing is almost absent.
- **Cost is not analysed.** Every study kept full pay, so cost per unit of output can be derived from per-worker output. That is the main question for any employer, and it is missing.

## How the four documents fit together

| Source | Per-hour gain (best estimate) | Per-worker change |
|---|---|---|
| Halden (as reported, scheduled hours) | +23.4% | −1.3% |
| Varga & Holm (corrected Halden subset) | +10.8% | −4.6% |
| Varden case-processing (randomised) | +12.5% | −2.1% |
| Meta-analysis, controlled discretionary | +9.6% | −2.7% |
| Meta-analysis, coverage-bound | +6.2% (likely utilisation) | −8.9% |

The picture is now consistent across the four documents:

- In discretionary work, output per actual hour rises by roughly **8–12%**, and output per worker falls slightly, by about **2–5%**.
- In coverage-bound work, output per worker falls by about **9–11%**, and service gets worse.
- The headline figures above 20% come from scheduled hours, manager ratings and uncontrolled designs.
- Sick leave falls by about 30%, which is the most consistent finding across all four documents.
- Durability beyond about a year is the main open question. The meta-analysis claims to have settled it but has not.

## Fair summary

Across 23 studies, reduced hours at full pay raise output per hour. The best-designed studies put the gain at about 8–10%, well below the 20%+ figures from uncontrolled pilots that used scheduled hours and manager reports. In discretionary work, output per worker is roughly maintained or falls slightly; in controlled studies overall, it falls by about 4%. In coverage-bound work, output per worker falls by about 9%, and the small per-hour gain probably reflects busier staff rather than better work.

The evidence rules out both "entirely artifact" and "sector-general". Four between-study data points don't establish that effects last beyond a year. The mechanism remains unknown, and the cost to employers has not been analysed.
